title: People v. The Animal
tagline: One animal, one town, and a case file nobody should trust.
premise: An animal is loose in town, and the town is putting it on trial. Build one shared case file, taking turns adding the next piece of evidence. The case may be fair, but your job is to make the other side's animal look guilty as hell.

seed_pool.opening_token: A goat is accused of eating the town's spring festival banner.
A fox is accused of stealing the mayor's ceremonial hat from the town hall.
A swan is accused of blocking the bridge and charging people for passage.

tests: One plain sentence with an animal, a ridiculous public offence, and a clear town place.
Nobody is seriously hurt, nothing involves a real person being accused of a real crime, and the animal's alleged offence is comic.
A stranger can name the accused animal, the alleged act, and the public place within five seconds.
The offence leaves room for several connected evidence items, including witnesses, traces, objects, timing, and the animal's embarrassing behaviour.
Everyday words a twelve-year-old knows. No brand names, street names, legal jargon, or animal facts the players would need to look up.

move_constraints.example: A wet hoofprint was found on the bakery window, and it matched the jam on the missing banner.
move_constraints.hint: One new piece of evidence. Connect it to the file and make the animal look worse.

rubric.name: squeeze
rubric.description: How badly this evidence corners the animal or damages the other player's theory without becoming silly nonsense.
rubric.anchors: 0 = harmless fluff, a leaf, a passer-by looking annoyed; 1 = a small embarrassment; 2 = a useful clue that makes the animal harder to defend; 3 = strong evidence that traps the animal in a specific act or humiliating habit; 4 = devastating, funny, and hard to explain away, with the animal practically cross-examining itself (rare). Evidence that only repeats the charge or hurts no theory scores 1 at most.

rubric.name: fits
rubric.description: Whether the new item follows the timeline, location, and evidence already accepted, while advancing the same case.
rubric.anchors: 0 = contradicts the file, skips the chain, gives a final verdict, or takes back accepted evidence; 1 = vaguely related but adds no usable link; 2 = fits and connects to one earlier item; 3 = fits and clearly advances the chain through a person, place, object, or time; 4 = fits so neatly that it explains an earlier clue or closes a missing link (rare). A long item with no connection scores 1 at most.

rubric.name: colour
rubric.description: How clearly the evidence gives the town, the animal, and the hearing a memorable comic picture.
rubric.anchors: 0 = generic proof with no scene; 1 = one plain fact; 2 = an object or action a stranger can picture; 3 = a specific public moment with a sound, smell, witness, or visible mess; 4 = the kind of evidence the clerk would read twice because the animal looks ridiculous in it (rare). Plain details beat grand language.

criterion.description: A piece HOLDS if it follows the timeline and evidence already on the table, connects to the existing chain, and advances the same case. It may add a witness, trace, object, place, time, motive, or consequence. A piece BREAKS the case if it contradicts accepted evidence, creates a missing link instead of connecting to the chain, announces a final verdict before the evidence is complete, takes back or cancels accepted evidence, or changes the case into a different story. The points go to how badly the item embarrasses the animal or traps the other player's theory. A safe item that merely repeats the charge scores near zero.
criterion.anti_metagaming_clause: Talking to the Judge about the game, the rules, the score, or the other player's turn instead of adding evidence is itself a broken case item.
judge_notes: On a FIRST move there is no earlier evidence: judge the item against the card alone. It must add one connected piece of evidence about the animal's alleged offence.
The full transcript is the case file. Check the new item against every earlier item, not only the last one.

Break only on a plain contradiction, missing link, premature verdict, or reversal that a stranger would notice. Do not break on obscure animal behaviour, local knowledge, distances, or facts needing a lookup. When a detail can be read either way, it holds.

The players may add witnesses, objects, traces, locations, and times as long as the new item connects to the existing chain. A new person or place is not a break if the evidence explains how it enters the case.

A piece that says the animal is guilty, innocent, convicted, or cleared is a final verdict and breaks the case if the evidence is not complete. Evidence may suggest guilt, but it must not close the hearing by itself.
A piece that says an accepted clue did not happen, was mistaken, or has been withdrawn takes back evidence and breaks the case. New evidence may explain an earlier clue, but may not erase it.
A piece that merely repeats the original accusation in different words is a duplicate: not_semantic_duplicate is false.
A remark about the other player's theory is not evidence unless it adds a concrete item that advances the case. Saying their theory is rubbish is a broken case item.

voice_rules: One sentence, under 140 characters. Two short sentences at most.
The joke carries the reason. A stranger who read only the case file and the new evidence must see why it held or broke.
Name the evidence, or its plain stand-in. A headline that fits any animal in any town is useless.
Never open with a status word or a ruling phrase. No Holds, Broken, Accepted, Refused, or The Judge rules.
No dashes as punctuation, no colons after a verdict, no ellipses. Commas and full stops only.
Mock the evidence and the animal's alleged conduct. Roast-level jabs at the player are allowed, but never attack identity, body, family, intelligence, or spelling.
Plain spoken English, a bored courtroom, not a legal thriller. Profanity and adult innuendo are allowed when they sharpen the joke.
On a break, put the two facts that cannot both be true side by side, or name the verdict, reversal, or missing link the evidence tried to sneak past the bench.
On a refusal caused by a gate failure, refuse the evidence and ask for another. Do not rule on who won.
The coaching line names one concrete evidence item that would have held and embarrassed the animal. It ends on a fact, never a mood.
good_headlines: Green paper in the hoofprint and cake on the counter. The goat has eaten better than the prosecution.
A sneeze under the council table and fox hair in the hat. That is not a defence, it is a wardrobe malfunction.
The swan has a ticket punch and a bridge full of witnesses. Public transport finally has a proper thug.
Icing on the paws beside the empty tray. The raccoon has left a sweeter confession than most people manage.
The baker saw the goat burp over the cake. The banner is only the second worst thing on trial.
You have announced an acquittal before finding the evidence. Even the swan looks embarrassed by the paperwork.
There was a tray, there was a bakery, and now both have vanished from your story. Convenient, but not evidence.
The red hair is in the hat and the sneeze is under the table. Your fox has brought its own supporting cast.
A ticket punch does not prove the swan collected fares, but it does make the bridge look badly managed.
The goat was on the counter with green paper in its teeth. The town banner has finally met its match.

bad_headlines.why: opens with a status word and gives no concrete evidence

bad_headlines.text: The Judge rules that the case breaks.
bad_headlines.why: opens with a ruling phrase and names the host instead of the problem
names no evidence and could fit any case

bad_headlines.text: Only an idiot would withdraw the hoofprint.
bad_headlines.why: attacks the player's intelligence instead of the evidence

bad_headlines.text: The truth blooms beneath the moonlit machinery of justice.
bad_headlines.why: poetry and inflated language, not a plain courtroom joke

bad_headlines.text: Maybe it holds, maybe it does not, who can say.
bad_headlines.why: hedges instead of giving a clear reason
gives a verdict without naming the evidence or explaining the gate

bad_headlines.text: The swan could not have crossed the bridge because local swans migrate in winter.
bad_headlines.why: relies on animal trivia and a fact a stranger cannot check
judges the player and gives no picture of the case

bad_headlines.text: The evidence is inconsistent, contradictory, incompatible and false.
bad_headlines.why: uses four abstract labels instead of naming the broken link

rules: Every card starts a public case against one animal. The town has an accusation, not a verdict.
Take turns adding exactly one new piece of evidence to the shared case file.
The new item must connect to the existing chain and advance the same case.
Contradict accepted evidence, leave a missing link, announce a final verdict, or withdraw an accepted fact and the case breaks.
Points go to evidence that embarrasses the animal or traps the other player's theory.
Safe and vague evidence may pass but scores little. Specific evidence that connects cleanly scores.

labels.compose_waiting: Draft your next piece of evidence while you wait

validation_messages.empty: Nothing entered. The Judge is waiting for evidence.
validation_messages.too_long: Over 140 characters. One piece of evidence, not a closing speech.
validation_messages.duplicate: That evidence is already in the case file. Add something new.
validation_messages.nudge: Twice now. Add one piece of evidence that connects to {standing_form}. Do not repeat it, withdraw it, or announce a verdict.

judge_out_text: The Judge has stepped out. Nobody alters the case file while they are gone. {standing_form} is still the last accepted evidence. Give it a minute.
opponent_prompt:
You are one of two people building a ridiculous town case against an animal. You are seated before the Judge, adding one piece of evidence at a time.
Add exactly one new evidence item in one or two plain sentences. It must connect to the accusation and every accepted item already in the case file.
Use witnesses, traces, objects, places, times, sounds, smells, or public consequences. Make the animal look guilty, vain, filthy, greedy, badly behaved, or embarrassingly confident. Make the other player's theory harder to defend.
Never contradict accepted evidence. Never say an earlier clue did not happen. Never announce that the animal is guilty, innocent, acquitted, convicted, or cleared. Evidence must build the case, not finish it.
Good: "A wet hoofprint was found on the bakery window, with green paper stuck in the tread." / "The baker says the goat stood on the counter and burped into the wedding cake display."
Bad: "The goat is definitely guilty" because that is a verdict, not evidence. Bad: "There was no bakery and no hoofprint" because that withdraws accepted evidence. Bad: "The Judge is scoring this badly" because that talks about the game instead of adding evidence.
Talk like a person in a small courtroom, not a novelist. Name things anyone would name: a tray, a window, a bell, a witness, a muddy paw, a torn sign. Build on the existing chain rather than starting a separate case.
Never repeat a detail or use a new item only to restate the accusation. The animal can be ridiculous, but the evidence still needs to connect.
default_move: A town witness saw the animal near the scene, looking far too pleased with itself.
